AL.summary: No Alabama law requires an officer to tell you why you were stopped before asking questions or for documents. You still must show your license, registration and proof of insurance when asked.
AL.inPractice: The U.S. Supreme Court has called explaining the reason good police practice but not a constitutional requirement (Devenpeck v. Alford, 2004). Any ticket or warning will list the violation, and you can calmly ask why.

CA.summary: Officers must tell you why they stopped you before asking questions about a traffic violation or crime (Veh. Code § 2806.5, since Jan. 1, 2024). You still must show license, registration and insurance when asked.
CA.inPractice: The only exception is when an officer reasonably believes holding back the reason is needed to protect life or property from an imminent threat. The reason must also be written on any ticket or report. Pedestrian stops count too.
CA.detail: Reason before questioning; in effect Jan. 1, 2024

CO.summary: Colorado law doesn't require it, but State Patrol policy tells troopers to give the reason for the stop when they ask for your documents. You still must show license, registration and insurance when asked.
CO.inPractice: A 2025 bill (HB25-1243) to require all officers to state the reason was rejected in committee. State law does require officers to hand a business card to drivers stopped but not ticketed or arrested.
CO.detail: State Patrol policy only; 2025 bill failed

CT.summary: Officers must tell you out loud why you were stopped, but only before the stop ends, not necessarily at the start (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-294oo, since June 2023). You still must show license, registration and insurance when asked.
CT.inPractice: The one-sentence law sets no penalty for officers who don't comply. Lawmakers who backed it described it as writing common courtesy into law.
CT.detail: Reason required before the stop ends

DE.summary: No Delaware law requires an officer to tell you why you were stopped before asking questions or for documents. You still must show your license, registration and proof of insurance when asked.
DE.inPractice: A pending bill (HB 196) would only have officers record the main reason for each stop in a state database; it wouldn't require telling you. It was last listed as out of committee (June 2025).

DC.summary: No D.C. law requires an officer to tell you why you were stopped before asking questions or for documents. You still must show your license, registration and proof of insurance when asked.
DC.inPractice: MPD academy training (2023) teaches officers to identify themselves and state the reason before asking for documents, but that's training guidance, not a binding law.

FL.summary: No Florida statute requires it, but Florida Highway Patrol policy says troopers will tell the driver the reason for the stop, a step listed before collecting documents. You still must show license, registration and insurance.
FL.inPractice: This is FHP internal policy (17.21, revised 2023) and covers state troopers only. Florida law separately requires you to carry your license and show it when an officer demands it (Fla. Stat. § 322.15).

GA.summary: No Georgia statute requires it, but Department of Public Safety policy tells state troopers to politely give the reason for the stop before asking for your license. You still must show license, registration and insurance.
GA.inPractice: This is internal policy (DPS Policy 11.03, revised 2018) for state troopers only; local police and sheriffs set their own rules. Federal law sets no duty to explain the reason first.

HI.inPractice: Hawaii has no state police; county departments set policy. Honolulu police policy says officers should greet you, identify themselves and give the reason before asking for documents, but that isn't state law.

MD.summary: At the start of a stop, unless there's an emergency, officers must show ID, give their name, ID number and agency, and tell you the reason for the stop (Crim. Proc. § 2-109). You still must show license, registration and insurance.
MD.inPractice: An officer who skips this can face discipline, but evidence can't be thrown out for that reason. A 2026 bill (HB 81) that would have allowed evidence to be excluded got a hearing but did not pass.
MD.detail: Reason at start of stop, absent exigent circumstances

MN.summary: On traffic stops, officers can't ask whether you know why you were pulled over; they must tell you the reason unless that would be unreasonable in the circumstances (Minn. Stat. § 169.905). You still must show your license when asked.
MN.inPractice: The 2024 law doesn't name an exact moment, but it replaces the classic opening question. It covers stops for traffic or registration violations, and a violation can't get evidence excluded or a ticket dismissed.
MN.detail: No "do you know why" question; enacted 2024
